parsed.hook: Tessellae is Lafage’s old-vine red built for people who want Roussillon ripeness without syrup. The blend of Syrah, Carignan, Grenache, and Monastrell points straight to the zone’s dry, sun-baked gravel and schist soils, where low yields give you dark fruit, dried herbs, and a tannic spine instead of jam.
parsed.wine_summary:
This wine matters because it sits at the sharp end of what Côtes Catalanes does best: mature Mediterranean fruit balanced by savory structure. Lafage works in a region where Carignan and Grenache are not decorative blending grapes but the backbone of the landscape, and the old-vine designation matters because older vines push roots deeper into poor soils and naturally crop low, which concentrates flavor. That is why Tessellae tends to read as black cherry, plum skin, thyme, olive, and dusty earth rather than simple sweet berry fruit.

The producer’s strength is knowing when to let ripe southern fruit stay firm. At 14.5% ABV in the vintages listed, this is not a light red, but alcohol alone does not define it; the point is whether the fruit has enough depth and the tannins enough grip to carry that ripeness. In good vintages, this lands as a serious value bottle for drinkers who like the savory edge of southern France more than polished international Cabernet styling.
parsed.terroir_expression: Côtes Catalanes spans the Roussillon side of the Pyrénées-Orientales, where the climate is hot, dry, and wind-exposed, with the Tramontane drying the vines after rain and limiting disease pressure. That matters because heat builds ripeness in Syrah, Grenache, and Monastrell, while drought keeps berries small and skins thick, which raises tannin and color concentration. The soils here vary widely, but the common denominator is poor drainage and low fertility — often schist, gneiss, clay-limestone, or gravelly alluvium — and those lean soils push the wine toward mineral dust, iron, and herbal bitterness rather than plush sweetness.
parsed.vinification_summary: Tessellae’s old-vine fruit is the kind of material that benefits from careful extraction, because Carignan and Syrah can turn hard if you overwork them. Carbonic maceration, when used, means fermenting whole berries in a carbon-dioxide-rich tank; that lowers harsh tannin and lifts red and black fruit, which is useful in a blend that already has natural grip. Even when the wine is made in a more traditional way, the goal is the same: keep the fruit dense, let the spice and earth speak, and avoid sanding off the Mediterranean edge that gives the wine its identity.
parsed.food_pairing:
Nashville hot chicken works because the wine’s ripe fruit cools the chile heat and its tannin scrubs the fried crust.
Duck confit with lentils de Puy works in a more formal setting: the wine’s dried herb and black olive notes meet the duck’s fat, while the lentils echo the earthy backbone.
Lamb merguez with couscous is a natural match; the spices lock onto the wine’s Syrah-driven pepper and the grain absorbs the alcohol.
Porchetta with rosemary potatoes lands well at a trattoria or steakhouse because the wine has enough body for the pork fat and enough savory lift for rosemary and garlic.
A fine-dining option is roast squab with mushrooms and a black olive jus, where the wine’s iron, earth, and dark fruit mirror the dish’s depth without needing obvious oak.
comparable_wines: Domaine de la Rectorie Côtes du Roussillon Villages — similar southern French structure, but usually a touch more maritime in feel and often more mineral than plush.
Mas Becha Côtes du Roussillon Villages — comparable old-vine Mediterranean blend with ripe fruit, herbal dryness, and a value-first price point.
Clos des Fées Les Sorcières — same Roussillon logic of sun, low yields, and savory fruit, though usually with a slightly more polished, modern profile.
parsed.style_profile: Old-vine Mediterranean red with medium-full body, firm tannins, and savory dark-fruit depth
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through the next 4 to 6 years if you like the fruit still vivid; older bottles may gain more olive, leather, and dried herb character. Store cool and steady, because this style loses its balance fast if heat pushes the alcohol forward.
parsed.value_assessment: At $14.56, this sits in the budget-to-entry-value red range, and it competes directly with Côtes du Rhône Villages, basic Priorat reds, and northern Spanish Garnacha around the $12 to $18 mark. It is worth the money because you are buying old-vine concentration and southern French savory complexity, not just ripe fruit.
parsed.market_position: This is a retail-shelf wine for shoppers who already know that Roussillon can outperform its price tag, and it belongs on restaurant lists by the glass or in the under-$60 bottle section. Casual drinkers who like Shiraz or Garnacha will get it quickly, while collectors use it as a weekday bottle that still tastes rooted in place.
parsed.insider_take: The tradeoff is simple: if you want polished, fruit-forward red with soft tannins, buy something else. Tessellae rewards drinkers who like a little dust, iron, and grip in the glass, and that savory edge is the whole point of the wine. People underrate how much old-vine Carignan changes the blend; without it, this would taste broader and less focused.
